cues.text: Watch F1 Finance's tax machine prepare HANGS General Contracting's quarterly unemployment insurance report.
First, it reads this year's earlier reports, and finds a bonus payroll left off the last one.
Next, 560 paychecks for 96 employees. Unemployment insurance is a state tax that funds benefits for laid-off workers. The company's rate is 3.1 percent.
Now it checks the state's official rules online. All fifteen checks are confirmed, and one question is left for a person.
Then it works out the tax. The taxable wage base is a yearly cap: only each employee's first $78,200 of pay is taxed. The tax comes to $38,682.
Ten checks pass: every wage line agrees with payroll.
Last, it writes the draft report and its workpapers, the math behind every figure.

All done. The draft shows $38,682 of unemployment tax for the quarter. Three items stay open. Last quarter's report left out a $55,500 bonus payroll, about $270 of tax. One worker paid as a vendor may really be an employee. And the report was due November 2: a person reviews, signs and files it, and pays. Nothing is filed or paid yet.
